description:
Je suis passionné par l’espace, la science et la technologie, et surtout par la façon dont les données de la NASA peuvent aider à résoudre des problèmes bien réels sur Terre : le climat, l’agriculture, l’eau, et surtout très passionné par l’IA

Mes compétences :  la programmation en Python, l’analyse de données, le design, la présentation orale.

Pourquoi rejoindre mon équipe ? Parce que je suis curieux, organisé, à l’écoute et que je m’investis jusqu’à la dernière minute du challenge.
summary: A web-based decision-support application for rain-fed agriculture in the Senegalese Sahel. Faced with erratic rainfall, farmers struggle to choose the right crop, the right variety, and the right sequence from one year to the next. NAZA addresses this problem by combining 20 years of climate data (2005-2024) from four sites (Thiès, Kaolack, Ziguinchor, Richard-Toll) with the requirements of 47 varieties and an agronomic reference base of 16 crops. For each site and each year, the application checks whether a variety can complete its cycle and avoid dry spells during flowering. It then ranks 3-year rotations using five criteria: average success rate, robustness in the worst years, soil nitrogen, suitability to the zone, and quality of crop successions. The stakes are high: choosing the right rotation protects yields, soil fertility, and producers’ income. The criteria are climate-based and will be validated with agronomists.
details:
How it works.

(1) Daily NASA POWER data (MERRA-2 reanalysis: rainfall, temperature, soil wetness and more) is downloaded for each site for 2005–2024; it is our main source for detecting season onset and end and for testing every variety.

(2) NASA GPM IMERG satellite rainfall is an independent check on POWER: it exposed a POWER artefact in 2020 at Richard-Toll (561 mm vs 0.6 mm for 20 Feb–15 Apr), which we corrected.

(3) NASA SMAP soil moisture confirms POWER soil wetness (correlation 0.84 to 0.95), so we can trust POWER for the soil-water part of the analysis.

(4) NASA MODIS NDVI (vegetation greenness) checks that the growing seasons we detect match what plants actually do.

(5) ISRIC SoilGrids (not NASA) gives soil pH and texture, used for crop limits and for the soil water reserve.

(6) Season onset and end are detected with rainfall rules; dry spells are counted during installation, mid-season and flowering.

(7) Crop needs come from published sources and an agronomic parameter table; each variety is tested against each site-year (3,760 checks).

(8) A per-site linear model predicts season length from the observed onset; it was validated by leave-one-year-out (RMSE 16.6 → 12.0 days). The team's live Streamlit app (https://jamm-agri-tech.streamlit.app/) turns this into a decision aid with four tools:

(a) a six-season rotation plan for a three-plot farm, with success rates and the reasons crops are excluded;

(b) at rain onset, a variety recommended for each plot with its probability of completing its cycle (80% threshold) and a simulated SMS message for the farmer;(c) a 20-year replay comparing a farmer alone with an advised farmer;

(d) a NASA data tab listing sources. Farm plots on the map are simulated for illustration. Results are preliminary and agronomic parameters still need expert validation.

Benefits. A transparent, data-based shortlist that farmers and extension services can check. It shows where rainfed farming is not viable (Richard-Toll: 0 varieties in 11 of 20 years) and which years were unfavorable everywhere (2016, 2019).

What we hope to achieve. Earlier, better-informed sowing decisions and a base that can be extended to more sites and crops.

Limits (stated honestly). No yield data, so the model predicts season length, not yield. Crop needs are not available per growth stage. Soil values need local validation. Some crop parameters are indicative and need validation with ISRA and ANACIM.

Tools. Python (pandas, numpy, scipy, matplotlib), Streamlit, GitHub, Streamlit Community Cloud, NASA POWER API, GPM IMERG via Earthdata, ISRIC SoilGrids, NASA SMAP, MODIS NDVI.
